newsitem.title: JAPAN: Defector rains on N.Korea Kim's birthday party.
newsitem.headline: Defector rains on N.Korea Kim's birthday party.

text.p: The surprise defection of Hwang Jang-yop, a close aide to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, is one more embarrassment, but not necessarily a fatal blow, to the beleaguered communist state, analysts said on Wednesday.

Hwang, the most senior North Korean official to ever defect to the rival South, sought asylum at the South Korean embassy in China on Wednesday, just four days before the birthday of Kim Jong-il and less than a week after he attended a big birthday party for Kim in Tokyo.

"The timing is bad, just before Kim Jong-il's 55th birthday on the 16th," said Noriyuki Suzuki of Radiopress, a Japanese news service which monitors North Korea. "It would be a big shock for Kim Jong-il."

North Korea, which in recent months has had to swallow its pride and seek international aid to fend off famine, would likely put a brave face on the defection of Hwang, a secretary at the communist country's ruling Workers' Party and a member of its central committee, Suzuki told Reuters.
"The damage to North Korea is big, maybe more than if any other politburo member had defected," he said.
"But that doesn't mean that the North Korean establishment will fall apart," said Suzuki, echoing Western analysts who say predictions of the demise of the world's last Stalinist state are premature.

The state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) remained predictably silent about the bombshell, continuing a stream of celebratory propaganda about "the greatest national holiday", as Kim's birthday is referred to.

North Korea watchers scrambled to determine why the leading ideologue of juche, Pyongyang's quirky blend of communism and virulent nationalism, chose to leave a system in which he was well-connected and well cared for.
Suzuki said Hwang may have been disgusted with the shift in official ideology from rugged self-reliance to "blind faith in the great leader".

Japanese media speculated that Hwang, who left Tokyo on Tuesday after a two-week visit to attend a seminar, may have feared going home after failing to win new pledges of food aid, badly needed after two years of floods and grain shortfalls.
But Japanese North Korea expert Masao Okonogi said the key question is "what now?".

"It will be very difficult to deal with this case. North Korea may never admit that Hwang defected, and may even start saying he was abducted -- and that would be a mess," Okonogi, professor at Tokyo's Keio University, told Reuters.
The pro-Pyongyang General Association of Korean Residents in Japan issued a terse denial on Wednesday, saying the official had boarded a train home from China.

The defection could pour cold water on expectations in Washington and Seoul that North Korea will agree to join them and China in four-way talks aimed at achieving a permanent peace on the tense Korean peninsula, Okonogi said.
"It may be difficult to hold the four-way talks," Okonogo said. "His defection says to the international community that a very senior official has given up on the future of North Korea."
Okonogi also predicted delays in Kim Jong-il's long-awaited assumption of power from his late father Kim Il-sung, North Korea's founder who died in July 1994.
"North Korea has been trying to prepare a smooth shift of power, but now Kim has to take up his father's role amid this confusion," he said. "It's quite a birthday present."
